belongs_to: Q4 "Tick in the appropriate cell for the following statements." (the blank tick table)
description: Blank tick table, 4 columns x 6 rows (1 header row + 5 statement rows), thick black outline and black grid lines. Header row has a light-green fill (the body cells are white/unfilled). Header cells: column 1 'Statement' (wide, about 60% of the table width, text centred, bold); column 2 'Always True' (two lines: 'Always' / 'True'); column 3 'Sometimes True' (two lines: 'Sometimes' / 'True'); column 4 'Never True' (two lines: 'Never' / 'True'); columns 2-4 are narrow and about equal width (column 3 slightly wider than 2 and 4). All header text is bold. The five statement rows, top to bottom, each left-aligned in the first column: row 1 'Adding 10 to a number gives a multiple of ten.' (one line); row 2 'Changing the order of the numbers in subtraction makes no difference.' (two lines, the break after 'in'); row 3 'In multiplication, doubling one number and halving the other keeps the product the same.' (two lines, justified, the break after 'and'); row 4 'Multiplication by an odd number gives an even number.' (two lines, the break after 'even'); row 5 "Multiplying a number by 5 leads to numbers which have '0' in the Ones place." (two lines, the break after 'which'). In every statement row the three answer cells (Always True / Sometimes True / Never True) are completely empty (no ticks, no marks): 5 rows x 3 empty cells = 15 empty cells for the student to tick one cell per row. Row heights: row 1 shortest (single line), rows 2-5 taller (two lines each); the header row is about as tall as a two-line row.

belongs_to: Q3 (a), (b), (c) "Think about the following statements and find examples as suggested below" - the red margin notes printed beside the three statements
description: Three red (hand-lettered, italic) margin annotations, each a short curved arrow with a text label at its tail, printed in the right margin beside Q3. Counted: 3 arrows. (1) Label 'Always true' at the right of the gap between (a) and (b); its thin curved arrow runs left from the label and ends with an open arrowhead pointing up-left at the end of the last line of statement (a) ('...the statement can be false?'), so it answers statement (a) "When two odd numbers are added, the sum is even." (2) Label 'Never true' at the right of the gap between (b) and (c); its curved arrow runs left and ends with an arrowhead pointing up-left at the end of the last line of statement (b) ('...Can you find any?'), so it answers statement (b) "Multiplying a number by 2 can give an odd number." (3) Label 'Sometimes true' placed below and to the right of the last line of (c); its curved arrow runs left and ends with an arrowhead pointing left at the end of the last line of statement (c) ('...when this is not true?'), so it answers statement (c) "Halving a number always leads to an even number." The arrows are the book's own classification hints (a = always true, b = never true, c = sometimes true) and carry no numbers; the three labels are the same three category words used as the column headings of the tick table in Q4 (Always true / Sometimes true / Never true).
unclear: Whether the book intends these margin arrows as part of the question figure or as decoration/hints: they name the answer category of Q3(a), (b), (c) but sit inside the question page, not in the printed solutions.
